title: Hyphema: A Comprehensive Clinical Roadmap
summary: Hyphema, the presence of red blood cells within the anterior chamber, is a common consequence of ocular trauma and systemic disease. This guide provides a high-yield, resident-level overview of classification, management protocols, and critical complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: A hyphema is the accumulation of red blood cells (RBCs) in the anterior chamber, typically settling inferiorly due to gravity. While most cases are traumatic, resulting from the rupture of iris or ciliary body vessels (e.g., the Major Arterial Circle), spontaneous cases must prompt investigation into iris neovascularization, uveitis, or hematological dyscrasias.

sections.title: Critical Pathophysiology
content: 1. Blunt force causes anteroposterior compression and equatorial expansion.
2. Rapid increase in intraocular pressure (IOP).
3. Posterior displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm.
4. Shearing of vessels at the Iris Root or Ciliary Body (Angle Recession).
5. Hemorrhage into the Aqueous Humor.

sections.title: The Sickle Cell Emergency
content: MANDATORY screening for Sickle Cell Trait/Disease (SCD) in all African American/Mediterranean patients.
AVOID Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs) - Methazolamide/Acetazolamide increase sickling via acidosis.
AVOID Hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol) - can cause hemoconcentration and sickling.
IOP Threshold for surgery is lower (>24 mmHg for >24 hours) due to risk of CRAO/Optic Atrophy.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Visual Acuity (initial and daily monitoring).
Slit-lamp exam: Assess Grade, Clot status (Red vs. Black), and Corneal Staining.
IOP measurement: Goldmann applanation is preferred (unless ruptured globe).
Deferred Gonioscopy: Perform at 2-4 weeks to assess for angle recession/PAS.
Dilated Fundoscopy: Rule out retinal tears, dialysis, or Berlin's edema (Commotio Retinae).
B-Scan Ultrasonography: If view is obscured to rule out RD or vitreous hemorrhage.

sections.title: Standard Medical Management
content: 1. Bed rest with Head of Bed elevated to 30-45 degrees (promotes settling).
2. Rigid Fox Shield at all times (prevent further trauma).
3. Cycloplegia (Atropine 1% BID/TID) to reduce iris movement and spasm.
4. Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1% QID) to reduce inflammation.
5. Antifibrinolytics (Aminocaproic Acid 50mg/kg q4h) - Consider in high-risk/pediatric cases to prevent rebleed.
6. IOP control: Beta-blockers or Alpha-agonists first-line.

sections.title: Indications for Surgical Intervention
content: Uncontrolled IOP: >50 mmHg for 2 days or >35 mmHg for 7 days.
Early Corneal Blood Staining: Any sign of endothelial pigment/haze.
Total Hyphema (8-Ball): If IOP > 35 mmHg for 5 days.
Persistence: Large clot remaining for >10 days (risk of PAS).
Sickle Cell: IOP >24 mmHg for >24 hours.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: 1. Simple Paracentesis: Burping the wound to lower IOP.
2. AC Washout: Two-port irrigation/aspiration of liquid blood.
3. Clot Express: Manual expression through a larger limbal incision (less common).
4. Automated Vitrectomy: Using a vitrector probe to remove organized clot (highest safety).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Aspirin and NSAIDs are STRICTLY contraindicated as they increase the risk of rebleeding.
An 8-ball hyphema is black because the blood is deoxygenated and trapped; it is not necessarily older than red blood.
Corneal blood staining begins in the deep stroma and can take years to clear, often from the periphery inward.
Angle recession is found in 70-100% of traumatic hyphema cases; long-term glaucoma follow-up is mandatory.

sections.title: Recent Evidence & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The 'Aminocaproic Acid vs. Placebo' trials demonstrated a significant reduction in rebleed rates (from 25-30% down to 3-4%) in high-risk populations. Recent Cochrane reviews emphasize that while systemic antifibrinolytics reduce rebleeds, they do not necessarily improve final visual acuity compared to standard conservative management. Current standard of care focuses on outpatient management for Grade I-II unless social factors or SCD are present.
